papers.title: How Does Capital Flow To Poor Countries? Evidence from Venture Capital and Private Equity
papers.abstract: Why does so little private capital flow to poor countries? We study how venture capital and private equity investors evaluate firms across countries, using an experimental survey of 1,485 investors in 108 countries who are incentivized to evaluate hypothetical investment opportunities with randomized firm characteristics, locations, and investment terms. Investors respond similarly to firm fundamentals, but otherwise comparable firms attract substantially less interest in poorer countries. This poor-country penalty is much smaller among investors specialized in emerging markets. Detailed survey data show that emerging market and developed market investors have largely similar investment practices, but differ in how they obtain country information, assess and manage country risks, and exit investments. Investors reporting active country-risk management apply smaller country penalties, even after accounting for market focus. Our findings suggest that investors' specialization and investment practices shape how country risk affects investment: the same firm can face drastically different financing prospects depending on where it is located and which investors evaluate it.

papers.title: Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field
papers.abstract: Neoclassical demand obeys regularity: adding a good can only draw demand away from existing goods. In a natural field experiment with Lyft covering 7.2 million riders and 47 million choices, we randomize the presence and price of a premium ride. Contrary to regularity, the premium ride raises demand for the cheapest incumbent and for not buying. The effect grows with the premium price and with repeated exposure, and persists in sessions where the premium ride is not displayed. Rational inference and inattention cannot account for these facts. A model in which a surprisingly high price, cued on the app and retrieved from memory, draws attention to prices explains them.

papers.title: Education and Gender Voting Polarization: The Effect of Compulsory Schooling on Sex-Based Preferences for the Democratic and Republican Parties
papers.abstract: One of the most notable developments in U.S. electoral politics over the last 40 years is the increasing divide between men and women voters. While men and women had roughly equivalent levels of support for both the Democratic and Republican parties in 1980, more recent surveys have revealed a roughly 10 to 15-percentage-point gap in preference for the Democratic party among women relative to men. We explain this result by using a variety of econometric strategies to establish a novel connection between compulsory schooling laws (CSLs), educational attainment, and diverging political preferences by sex. First, we show that the timing of this divergence is coincident with recent changes in CSLs, and that this divergence is almost entirely due to changes in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party in states where there exists a much stronger effect of CSLs on average educational attainment -- very little change in sex-related preferences for the Democratic party is present in other states. Furthermore, in states with more-impactful CSLs, changes in CSLs and their associated increased educational attainment explain almost all of the diverging support for political parties and differences in opinion over major policy issues by sex, such as gun control and abortion. Altogether, these new facts present an original explanation that relies upon the effect of education to explain the evolution of gender political preferences in the U.S. over the last 40 years.

papers.title: fereg: Fast High-Dimensional Fixed-Effects Regressions in Stata
papers.abstract: Regressions with many fixed effects are central to applied research, but fitting them to large datasets can be slow. In this article, I present the commands fereg and feppml, which fit linear and Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood regressions with high-dimensional fixed effects. Both commands use familiar Stata syntax and pass the computation to a compiled plugin. The plugin chooses among projection, Krylov, and multigrid solvers according to the structure of the fixed effects, checks every result before posting it, and runs on several processor cores. The commands support multiple and interacted fixed effects, group-specific slopes, regression weights, robust and multiway clustered standard errors, saved fixed effects, and prediction. Two simulated examples illustrate their use. In simulated designs with up to ten million observations and default stopping settings, fereg was 6–204 times faster than reghdfe and feppml 11–103 times faster than ppmlhdfe. The commands were also faster than fixest (R) and PyFixest (Python) in all 53 simulated configurations and than the Julia packages FixedEffectModels.jl and GLFixedEffectModels.jl in 52 of 53, with geometric-mean time ratios between 3.0 and 7.7. On administrative data with 1.2 million workers and 117,000 firms, fereg and feppml were at least 3.4 times faster than every other command at every number of cores.

papers.title: The Role of Parental Beliefs and Public Policies in Financing Higher Education: An Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Parents who want to financially support their child’s pursuit of higher education must save against assumptions about what college will cost and how it will be funded. This study examines how parental beliefs and future borrowing costs shape college saving decisions. Through a survey experiment with an embedded financial planning tool, we elicit parental beliefs about the future costs of college and their expectations of different funding sources, including financial aid and student loans. We find that nearly all parents want to cover some of the future costs of college, but many may fall short in their savings due to underestimating future expenses and overestimating available financial aid. A corrective information intervention encourages most parents to recalibrate their saving target. However, when a substantial gap between expected and actual costs is combined with a salient high repayment burden for their child, we find a discouragement effect that diminishes both their willingness to save and their aspirations for their child’s educational attainment. We calibrate a model of parental saving with learning about college costs, which reproduces both the absence of an average response to borrowing costs and the shift of children away from college attendance, and use it to price the welfare cost of misperception. Parents with higher financial literacy hold better-calibrated beliefs and respond more to correction. We discuss policy implications for outreach activities to support informed financial planning for college education.

papers.title: Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences
papers.abstract: Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities. Although providing information raises fairness concerns, it does not increase support for reforms reducing it, revealing an important political constraint to improving tax equity.

papers.title: Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement
papers.abstract: Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. We conduct the first randomized controlled trial of an impact measurement intervention among high-growth social enterprises in India. Treated firms exhibit nearly twice as much revenue growth and raise nearly twice as much capital as control firms. In a companion experiment with early-stage investors, we find that investors respond strongly to quantified impact metrics but not to generic qualitative impact statements. Together, our results show that impact measurement can shape firm growth and capital allocation.
